The graphite/epoxy composite plate had in-plane dimensions of 73 mm x 225 mm and a thickness of approximately 2.9 mm.
The layup of the composite plate was (±45/0₂)₃S.
Impact damage was introduced using a 9 kg impactor dropped from a height of 0.5 m onto the back face of the clamped specimen.
C-scan analysis showed the spanwise length of the damaged region was approximately 40 mm.
Vibration analysis using single point accelerometer response, holographic interferometry, and thermoelastic analysis was investigated for detecting BVID.
Accelerometer response data was analyzed in frequency ranges of 0-500 Hz, 0-2000 Hz, and 0-5000 Hz.
Estimated damping values for modes in the 300-370 Hz region were around 0.3-0.5% of critical damping.
Estimated damping values for modes in the 1050-1150 Hz region increased from 0.4-0.7% in the undamaged case to 0.9% in the damaged case.
Holographic interferometry showed that changes in boundary conditions appeared to dominate changes due to damage, but damage could be observed as perturbations to nearby fringes.
Thermoelastic analysis was only suitable for low frequency modes, as obtaining reasonable displacements for higher frequency modes was difficult with this specimen.

Further investigation of vibration analysis for BVID detection would require larger specimens to reduce boundary condition effects, or keeping boundary conditions constant while applying damage in-situ.
The sensitivity of the vibration analysis to changes in boundary conditions and excitation methods was a key limitation in detecting BVID in this study.
The researchers concluded that a better means of excitation would also be required to improve the detectability of BVID using vibration analysis.
The study demonstrated the challenges in using vibration-based techniques to reliably detect BVID in graphite/epoxy composite structures.
The results suggest that further research is needed to develop more effective non-destructive evaluation methods for detecting BVID in composite aircraft structures.
